passages.text: Cubism is one of the most revolutionary art movements of the twentieth century. Its influence reaches across artistic mediums throughout history. What is cubism in art? In this article, we’ll dive deep into this question by analyzing the origins of cubist art, the artists who pioneered the artistic movement, as well as why the philosophy of cubism left a profound impact on art itself. What is Cubism in Art? First, let’s define cubism Cubism can be a rather large subject to tackle, let alone to fully understand. The best place to start understanding the cubist art movement is with the cubism definition. For more, check out our index of art styles and our art history timeline covering more specific and noteworthy movements. CUBISM DEFINITION What is cubism in art? Cubism is an influential art style defined by its revolutionary method of depicting three-dimensional reality through geometrical shapes on a two-dimensional canvas. Established around 1907 or 1908, cubist artists depict a subject by utilizing geometrical shapes and forms from varying perspectives of the subject. passages.text: Cubism Art Movement – Overview, Definition, History and Evolution Cubism was an early-20th-century art movement developed in Paris by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, then extended by artists including Juan Gris, Fernand Léger, Jean Metzinger, Albert Gleizes, and Sonia and Robert Delaunay. Rather than copying appearances from one fixed viewpoint, Cubist artists compressed space, fractured forms, and tested how signs and everyday materials could represent objects. This article defines Cubism, traces its main phases and public networks, explains how to recognize its visual logic, and distinguishes core Cubists from precursors and later artists influenced by the movement. What Is Cubism? Cubism is a modern art movement that emerged from the close collaboration between Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in Paris from 1907 onward. They rejected the idea that a painting should behave like a window onto a continuous, three-dimensional world. Instead, they emphasized the flat surface by breaking figures, objects, and surroundings into interlocking planes, compressing depth, and combining different visual clues in one image. Cubism did not simply turn subjects into cubes. Its central innovation was a new relationship among object, space, and picture surface: forms can be fragmented, shifted, overlapped, and still remain recognizable through carefully placed clues.

Synthetic cubism is often recognized as a collage which utilizes other forms such as bits of a newspaper or other pieces to deepen the exploration and interpretation of a subject. The synthetic style utilizes words and even three-dimensional materials later known as assemblages (rather than sculptures). While synthetic cubism allowed artists to more deeply explore a subject, it was often associated with the lower artistic status of advertising due to its use of text in the image. Juan Gris: Le Petit Déjeuner (Breakfast) (1914) Analytical cubism art is often described as the more rigid or austere form compared to synthetic cubism. However, it is important to understand the level of experimentation that occurred during the movement. Artists were less concerned with the appearance of a final work, but rather interested in the process of exploring a subject through cubism. Therefore, it is important to see synthetic cubism as an evolution of what came before through deeper experimentation. To better understand how these iconic cubist artworks were created, it’s critical to understand the philosophical approach behind it. This double role is central to Synthetic Cubism. This framework also clarifies boundaries. A painting may show Cubist influence without belonging to the historical movement, and a geometric abstract work may pursue a different problem altogether. Orphism redirects Cubist structure toward color and light; Paul Klee learned from Cubism without joining a Cubist group; Cézanne was a precursor whose work helped make Cubism possible. Key Cubist Artists, Associates, and Precursors Cubism was not a single club with a fixed membership. Picasso and Braque developed its initial visual language; Gris and several Salon Cubists transformed it; Cézanne provided an essential precedent; and artists such as Klee absorbed Cubist lessons without becoming members of the movement. Cubism Meaning Understanding Cubism The cubist movement was an exciting and revolutionary approach to creating art because of the doors it opened for both artists and viewers. Rather than depicting a subject according to spatial logic, cubist artists explore a subject through varying perspectives and vantage points to fully understand it. Take a look at this video analysis of Pablo Picasso’s Night Fishing. Take note of how the method of cubism allows more depth to be depicted of the subject. How To Understand A Picasso • Cubism Meaning By exploring every possible angle of a subject, both the artist and the viewer can better discover that subject’s essence rather than its surface-level appearance. Cubism opened the doors to how artists can create an experience through their work rather than simply depicting a realistic form. In creating and observing this type of artwork, artists and art lovers can better understand the world around them. Le garçon au gilet rouge (‘The Boy in a Red Vest’, 1888-1890) by Paul Cézanne; Paul Cézanne, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Boy in a Red Vest (1888-1890) Boy in a Red Vest belongs to a series of portraits of the model Michelangelo di Rosa. The figure is not fragmented in the manner of later Cubism, but Cézanne’s color patches, elongated anatomy, and carefully tensioned relationship between body and surrounding space help explain why younger artists studied him. The painting is best used as evidence of Cézanne’s broader formal precedent, not as a Cubist work or a documented direct source for one specific Cubist canvas. Ad Parnassum (1932) by Paul Klee; Paul Klee, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Frequently Asked Questions What Is Cubism? Cubism is an early-20th-century modern art movement developed by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in Paris. Cubist works challenge fixed perspective by compressing space and organizing figures and objects through shifting planes, contrasting viewpoints, and representational clues. Later Cubists also used collage and everyday printed materials.

Its central innovation was a new relationship among object, space, and picture surface: forms can be fragmented, shifted, overlapped, and still remain recognizable through carefully placed clues. The Features of Cubist Paintings Many Cubist works disrupt the single, stable viewpoint associated with linear perspective. A contour may be shown from the front in one passage and from the side in another; a tabletop may tilt upward while a bottle remains upright; background and foreground may interlock rather than recede. This does not mean that every Cubist painting mechanically records all sides of an object at once. Multiple or contrasting viewpoints are one part of a broader effort to represent what artists knew and experienced about a subject, not only its appearance at a single instant. Still Life before an Open Window, Place Ravignan (1915) by Juan Gris; Philadelphia Museum of Art, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Cubist artists also made the viewer work between abstraction and recognition. Rythme, Joie de vivre (1930) by Robert Delaunay; Robert Delaunay, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons How to Recognize and Analyze Cubism Angular shapes are not enough to identify a historical Cubist work. A practical reading should test how space, object clues, and material signs operate together: - Read the space before naming the subject. Look for a shallow field in which forms overlap, tilt, or press forward. Check whether a tabletop, face, or instrument combines incompatible viewpoints and whether figure and ground share the same planes. - Find the clues that preserve representation. A curve may indicate a guitar, a scroll may identify a violin, and printed letters may evoke a newspaper or café sign. Cubism often makes recognition provisional rather than eliminating the subject. - Ask what is real and what is represented. Cubism introduced collage as a modern art form. In France and other countries Futurism, Suprematism, Dada, Constructivism, De Stijl and Art Deco developed in response to Cubism.[4] Early Futurist paintings hold in common with Cubism the fusing of the past and the present, the representation of different views of the subject pictured at the same time or successively, also called multiple perspective, simultaneity or multiplicity,[8] while Constructivism was influenced by Picasso's technique of constructing sculpture from separate elements.[9] Other common threads between these disparate movements include the faceting or simplification of geometric forms, and the association of mechanization and modern life. passages.text: Cubism Cubism is an early-20th-century avant-garde art movement which began in Paris. It revolutionized painting and the visual arts, and sparked artistic innovations in music, ballet, literature, and architecture. Cubist subjects are analyzed, broken up, and reassembled in an abstract form. Instead of depicting objects from a single perspective, the artist depicts the subject from multiple perspectives to represent the subject in a greater context.[1] Cubism has been considered the most influential art movement of the 20th century.[2][3] The term cubism is broadly associated with a variety of artworks produced in Paris (Montmartre and Montparnasse) or near Paris (Puteaux) during the 1910s and throughout the 1920s. The movement was pioneered in partnership by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, and joined by Jean Metzinger, Albert Gleizes, Robert Delaunay, Henri Le Fauconnier, Juan Gris, and Fernand Léger.[4] One primary influence that led to Cubism was the representation of three-dimensional form in the late works of Paul Cézanne.[2] A retrospective of Cézanne's paintings was held at the Salon d'Automne of 1904, current works were displayed at the 1905 and 1906 Salon d'Automne, followed by two commemorative retrospectives after his death in 1907.[5] In France, offshoots of Cubism developed, including Orphism, abstract art and

Undoubtedly, due to the great success of the exhibition, Cubism became avant-garde movement recognized as a genre or style in art with a specific common philosophy or goal.[51] Crystal Cubism: 1914–1918 [edit] A significant modification of Cubism between 1914 and 1916 was signaled by a shift towards a strong emphasis on large overlapping geometric planes and flat surface activity. This grouping of styles of painting and sculpture, especially significant between 1917 and 1920, was practiced by several artists; particularly those under contract with the art dealer and collector Léonce Rosenberg. The tightening of the compositions, the clarity and sense of order reflected in these works, led to its being referred to by the critic Maurice Raynal as 'crystal' Cubism.
